{"id": "29:48/q08", "question": "Did Muhammad later read or write, and how do the reported acts fit this verse?", "turns_on": "The time limit of 'before it', the force of hadiths saying 'he wrote', their reliability, and whether later writing would conflict with or add to the miracle of illiteracy.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q08/p1", "position": "He never personally read or wrote; reports of writing mean that he ordered a scribe, and reports of literacy are weak.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects the reports of al-Shaʿbī, Abū Kabsha and al-Bājī as weak. Qurṭubī prefers that he wrote no letter or read or spelled anything and notes twenty-six revelation scribes; Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ cites Muʿāwiya receiving letter-form instructions while writing for him. A later scholar argues writing would cancel the miracle of illiteracy. Most scholars, according to Abū Ḥayyān, treat 'he wrote' as ordinary agency, like a ruler writing through a scribe. Ibn Kathīr compares the Bukhārī and other Hudaybiyya wordings, says the Prophet remained unable to write a line, and calls the report of learned writing baseless. Al-Baghawī's Tahdhīb chooses this as sounder. Qurṭubī answers the Dajjāl objection with Ḥudhayfa's report that any believer can read its mark. Ālūsī says 'before it' preceding the writing negation nearly indicates he never wrote, though he calls the figurative account contrary to the hadith's apparent wording."}, {"id": "29:48/q08/p2", "position": "He personally wrote, or learned to read and write, after his earlier unlettered state.", "reasons": "Al-Shaʿbī is reported to say he wrote before death; Abū Kabsha reports that he read and explained ʿUyayna's document. Al-Barāʾ and Bukhārī's Hudaybiyya reports say he erased 'Messenger of God' and wrote 'son of ʿAbd Allāh'; one Bukhārī route also says he did not know writing. Al-Sumnānī, Abū Dharr, al-Bājī and others accept personal writing; al-Bājī was denounced and later defended his view before scholars. Ālūsī cites Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ via Nawawī that 'he could not write, then wrote' is nearly explicit. Some argue 'before it' scopes both negations and implies later literacy, but Ālūsī says that inference relies on an implication their advocate rejects. Abū al-ʿAbbās Aḥmad ibn ʿUmar says the reports are solitary and nondefinitive, so proponents should not be charged with unbelief. Ālūsī observes that the unlettered-community hadith need only describe early conditions and ultimately leaves the dispute to God."}, {"id": "29:48/q08/p3", "position": "A personally written mark could have been a new miracle without learned literacy.", "reasons": "Al-Sumnānī says God could move the Prophet's hand and pen to make intelligible marks without study, like knowledge given without learning; supporters cite the hadith that the community neither writes nor calculates. Ibn Kathīr suggests al-Bājī may have meant miraculous Hudaybiyya writing and compares the Dajjāl's written kafir mark, also pronounced as three letters. Ālūsī says learning writing after being unlettered would not erase the first miracle, while untrained writing would itself be another."}, {"id": "29:48/q08/p4", "position": "The verse leaves post-revelation literacy open; God might have taught him later.", "reasons": "Al-Murtaḍā restricts the explicit negation to before prophethood and says either later literacy or continued illiteracy is possible, even through Gabriel's teaching. Qāḍī ʿIyāḍ allows granted knowledge of writing while he was kept from actually reading and writing; he doubts the report of personal writing. Ālūsī says the unlettered-community hadith does not explicitly establish lifelong inability."}, {"id": "29:48/q08/p5", "position": "He could miraculously perceive written meaning without ordinary reading.", "reasons": "Ālūsī says God could grant reading without writing to account for the Night Journey report of the inscription at Paradise's gate promising charity tenfold and a loan eighteenfold; alternatively the report may omit his asking its meaning. An unidentified book says letters told him their names, as the poisoned foreleg spoke, but Ālūsī rejects this without a sound report."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q09", "question": "Why specify the right hand?", "turns_on": "Whether the expression primarily stresses the normal physical instrument or uses it as a metonym for personal action.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q09/p1", "position": "It vividly and literally emphasizes writing with the usual instrument, the right hand.", "reasons": "Kashshāf, Bayḍāwī and Ālūsī say naming the hand strengthens the denial and excludes figurative attribution. Nasafī, Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr invoke ordinary right-handed writing; Bursawī says this does not rule out rare left-handed writing. Biqāʿī points to the stronger hand; Ibn Kathīr and Ibn ʿĀshūr compare a bird flying with its wings at 6:38. Ṭabāṭabāʾī compares 'I saw with my eyes.' Abū Ḥayyān says the mention reinforces the proof."}, {"id": "29:48/q09/p2", "position": "Right hand can stand for one's own hand.", "reasons": "Asad calls yamīn, literally right hand, a metonym for personal writing."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q10", "question": "How is idhan and the consequence construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q10/p1", "position": "It answers an implicit condition: had he read or written before, the falsifiers would have doubted.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ, Nasafī, Burhān and Ibn ʿĀshūr reconstruct an omitted law condition. Majāz expands the compressed clause with a pronoun: 'if you had read the book and written it.' Samīn takes the same counterfactual sense. Burhān compares an implicit conditional about supposed other gods. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Qurayẓ al-ʿAnbarī's camel-raiding poem, al-Marzūqī's imagined question, and another possible second answer to law; he compares the saying 'if free, I would condemn slaves' deeds; then I would admire free men's deeds.'"}]}
{"id": "29:48/q11", "question": "What does irtiyāb mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the counterfactual describes first doubt or stronger doubt among those already suspicious.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q11/p1", "position": "Doubt or the occurrence of suspicion.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Mukhtār gloss the root as doubt; Jishumī adds suspicion; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes doubt arising in the mind, and distinguishes preliminary suspicion from justified denial. Al-Rāghib, quoted by Bursawī, contrasts rayb as a suspicion exposed as false with irāba as one not removed and treats irtiyāb like irāba, citing 74:31."}, {"id": "29:48/q11/p2", "position": "For opponents already in doubt, it means their suspicion would increase.", "reasons": "Farrāʾ gives this explanation as reported by Wāḥidī; Wāḥidī applies it especially to Quraysh, whose existing suspicion would grow."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q12", "question": "Who are al-mubṭilūn in this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the relevant doubt is an accusation of copying from Meccan opponents or a mismatch with the scriptural description known to the People of the Book.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q12/p1", "position": "The Quraysh or Meccan polytheists.", "reasons": "Mujāhid repeatedly names Quraysh; Qatāda and others are also cited. Their hypothetical accusation is that Muhammad learned from someone or copied earlier books. Ālūsī prefers this identification. Study Quran transmits it alongside the People-of-the-Book view."}, {"id": "29:48/q12/p2", "position": "Opposing People of the Book, especially Jewish unbelievers.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Suddi and others identify Jews; Farrāʾ names Christians familiar with the description. Wāḥidī prefers the People of the Book because they knew the unlettered prophet from scripture yet denied him. Qatāda is cited by Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others for Jews or the People of the Book. Some say the Torah or Gospel would contradict a literate claimant."}, {"id": "29:48/q12/p3", "position": "Deniers among both the People of the Book and the Arabs, or opponents generally.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī explicitly includes both groups. Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās's generic 'unbelievers'; Elmali describes unfair deniers seeking a pretext rather than fair-minded seekers. Farrāʾ also allows liars in Mecca and elsewhere."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q13", "question": "What does mubṭilūn mean, and why call them that?", "turns_on": "Whether the label points simply to false claims or specifically to how remaining evidence makes their denial baseless even under the hypothetical.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q13/p1", "position": "People who assert falsehood, deny truth, or try to invalidate it.", "reasons": "Wāḥidī says a mubṭil lies or claims contrary to truth and applies it to adherents of other religions; Ibn al-Jawzī says they bring falsehood; Bursawī contrasts muḥiqq and quotes Mufradāt that ibṭāl removes or destroys, citing 8:8. Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors those who call truth false; Asad cites lexicons allowing false claims, attempts to nullify, and judgments that something is unfounded, regardless of the target's actual truth. Nasafī, Ālūsī, Elmali and Ibn ʿĀshūr apply it to denial of prophethood and revelation; Ibn ʿĀshūr links the label with disbelievers in 29:47."}, {"id": "29:48/q13/p2", "position": "The label marks their denial as baseless even in the counterfactual of a literate Prophet.", "reasons": "Kashshāf and Ālūsī say illiteracy leaves no actual ground for doubt. Yet Kashshāf, Ālūsī, and Elmali point to other prophets' miracles and the Qur'an's inimitability: literacy would remove one evidential advantage, not excuse rejection. Al-Kashf calls the conditional illustrative of the miracle's role. Ibn ʿĀshūr says such doubt might be preliminary but certainty of denial remains unwarranted after examining the Qur'an's style and meaning."}]}

{"id": "29:48/q15", "question": "What does the verse establish about the Qur'an's origin and Muhammad's mission?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q15/p1", "position": "His unlettered condition together with the Qur'an's content shows revelation from God and supports his prophethood.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī says he had no historical teachers or scriptures yet told history from Adam onward, citing 6:105. Ibn ʿAṭiyya stresses the Qur'an's length, inimitability and unseen reports. Ṭabrisī points to people who watched him and saw no teacher. Qurṭubī and Naḥḥās add he did not mingle with People of the Book in Mecca yet conveyed earlier prophetic accounts; Bayḍāwī cites its noble sciences. Rāzī calls the unlettered delivery itself a miracle, links 2:23's 'someone like him' to his inability, and invokes 2:1. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds 42:52 and 10:16; Asad says this should persuade an unbiased reader. {"id": "29:48/q16", "question": "How does this verse advance the argument of the surrounding passage?", "turns_on": "Which nearby passage or broader Qur'anic feature is being connected to this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q16/p1", "position": "It adds the Prophet's unlettered delivery to the preceding proof that the Qur'an is revealed.", "reasons": "Rāzī says 29:47 had argued by analogy from the miracle proving earlier books revealed; this verse supplies another miracle. Burhān associates the disjoint opening letters with his lack of writing training; it counts fourteen of an alphabet it regards as twenty-nine, explains the extra letter and the alif/hamza naming, one omitted letter for concision, and twenty-nine opening-letter sūras with some forms avoided for difficult pronunciation."}, {"id": "29:48/q16/p2", "position": "The context of 29:50–51 concerns requested signs, so 29:51 is a poor heading for the hadith on melodic Qur'an recitation.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr rejects Bukhārī's chapter placement on the basis of 29:48–51's argumentative context."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q17", "question": "Can an unlettered person read without writing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q17/p1", "position": "Yes; unlettered can describe someone who reads but cannot write.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports this definition from Ibrāhīm, differing from Qatāda's definition of one who does not write and the accounts that the Prophet could neither read nor write."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q18", "question": "How did scholars receive al-Bājī's claim of the Prophet's writing?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q18/p1", "position": "Jurists strongly condemned the claim.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says jurists in East and West denounced those who followed al-Bājī and disassociated themselves from that position."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q19", "question": "What apparent objection from the Dajjāl report was raised against lifelong illiteracy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q19/p1", "position": "The Prophet reportedly spelled the letters of kafir inscribed between the Dajjāl's eyes.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī records this as an objection, then invokes Ḥudhayfa's report that every believer, whether literate or not, can read the mark."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q20", "question": "What further conclusions are drawn from preventing suspicion?", "turns_on": "These are separate inferences from the same preventive rationale, not competing accounts of the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q20/p1", "position": "A messenger's protection from acts that repel acceptance implies still stronger protection from major sins and transgression.", "reasons": "Jishumī says God prevented reading and writing to secure acceptance of the caller, lawgiver and explainer; avoidance of major sins and fisq follows even more strongly."}, {"id": "29:48/q20/p2", "position": "The conditional variation in doubt shows doubt is a human act rather than an act created by God.", "reasons": "Jishumī argues that if God created doubt it would persist independent of the Prophet's literacy; he uses this against the Mujbira's account of creation and capacity."}]}
{"id": "29:48/q21", "question": "What inward significance is given to his inability to read?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "29:48/q21/p1", "position": "Divine love and election left him free of otherness so revelation could address him.", "reasons": "Abū Saʿīd al-Kharrāz, reported by Sulamī, says love erased customary forms and natural traces; when first commanded to read he answered that he could not, then found ease in the command to read in his Lord's name at 96:1."}]}

{"id": "29:64/q06", "question": "Why does lahw precede laʿib here?", "turns_on": "The proposed contextual triggers differ: provision, current attraction, contrasting life stages, or the sura's call to strive.", "positions": [{"id": "29:64/q06/p1", "position": "The nearby mention of provision makes distraction by wealth especially relevant.", "reasons": "Samarrai's two works cite 29:62 and 63:9 on wealth and children diverting believers from God's remembrance; he says the reversed order is deliberate and this verse is exceptional among Qur'anic instances."}, {"id": "29:64/q06/p2", "position": "The immediate setting makes worldly absorption more likely, so its term comes first.", "reasons": "Razi contrasts 6:32, where people in regret are far from absorption; here worldly life's attraction is present."}, {"id": "29:64/q06/p3", "position": "Amusement's longer period, youth, comes before shorter childhood play to suit the contrast with lasting afterlife.", "reasons": "Burhan says the usual order follows childhood play then youthful amusement; 57:20 lists life stages. {"id": "29:64/q12", "question": "What does al-ḥayawān mean when predicated of the Hereafter?", "turns_on": "The word is explained as deathless life, life itself used intensively, an animate being, or a spring name; several authors give more than one sense.", "positions": [{"id": "29:64/q12/p1", "position": "True, enduring life without death or extinction.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Abbas and Dahhak are repeatedly reported; Tabari adds no disappearance or interruption. Ibn Jawzi says Paradise lacks worldly defects. Wahidi's al-Farra and al-Kalbi say no death; Ibn Atiyya approves Mujahid's gloss.
